summary.one_line: A leveraged, trader-sourced shrimp and dried-chilli processor from Andhra Pradesh with growing profits but three straight years of negative operating cash flow, a China-heavy export book and a patchy compliance record, raising ₹53.1 crore mainly to double shrimp capacity in a plant that will not run until April 2028 while the current one is under-utilised: avoid.
bull_points: Profit has compounded quickly: PAT rose from ₹665.99 lakh in FY24 to ₹1,035.20 lakh in FY25 and ₹1,561.12 lakh in FY26, with PAT margin widening from 2.10% to 4.07% and EBITDA margin from 5.47% to 6.57% (S2).
Leverage is falling: debt/equity improved from 4.12x (FY24) to 2.90x (FY25) and 2.40x (FY26), and net worth grew from ₹1,546.28 lakh to ₹4,142.62 lakh (S2).

The industry tailwind is real. India's frozen shrimp exports reached a record ₹49,037.93 crore in FY26, up 13.16% in rupee terms (S12). The US cut its tariff on Indian goods to 18% in February 2026, easing the 2025 tariff shock, when reports put the effective duty on Indian shrimp near 58% (S13, S15).

Most of the fresh issue goes to hard assets rather than to promoters. ₹4,002.77 lakh funds a shrimp plant on land that has already been bought and paid for from internal accruals (₹124.17 lakh). The OFS is small, at ₹700 lakh (S1, S2).
bear_points: Operating cash flow was negative in every year: -₹1,499.90 lakh (FY24), -₹505.82 lakh (FY25) and -₹626.63 lakh (FY26). Over the same years the company reported cumulative PAT of about ₹3,262 lakh (S2). Receivable days rose from 26 to 77 (S1).

The capex case is weak. The existing shrimp plant ran at only 38.38% net block-freezing utilisation and 13.00% IQF utilisation in FY26 (S1). No machinery orders have been placed. Commercial production of the new plant is targeted for April 2028 (S1).

Governance flags: 31 ROC forms were filed late, by up to 1,887 days. The company carried out processing for about 2.5 years before its objects clause allowed it, and its first condonation application was rejected. Statutory dues were paid late by up to 142 days (S1).

The balance sheet carries a ₹788.69 lakh contingent income-tax demand under s.68 (unexplained credits), equal to 19% of FY26 net worth. The company has not yet paid the full 10% pre-deposit, citing 'operational cash flow constraints' (S1).

Related-party and concentration risk: 31.29% of revenue comes from China and 77.85% from the top ten customers. The largest FY26 shrimp supplier is promoter-linked Green Asia Marine LLP (₹2,377.66 lakh). Former promoter firm SG Exports was a major customer (S1, S2).
watch_points: Final-day subscription on 28 September 2026. At the day-2 close the issue was only 0.03x subscribed, and QIB demand was 0.00x (S7).
Whether machinery orders for the Chinnayagudem plant are placed on the March–April 2027 schedule, and the quarterly monitoring-agency reports from Brickwork Ratings (S1).
The outcome of the AY 2022-23 income-tax appeal, where the demand is ₹788.69 lakh as a contingent liability and ₹901.19 lakh in the litigation section (S1).
Receivable collection in FY27, especially the ₹8,573.15 lakh of domestic receivables at March 2026, and whether operating cash flow turns positive (S1).

reasoning: The money raised does little for the next 18 months and targets the wrong bottleneck. ₹4,002.77 lakh of the ₹5,310 lakh fresh issue goes to a second shrimp plant with commercial production targeted for April 2028. Machinery orders are not yet placed and several site approvals are still pending (S1). The existing plant ran at just 38.38% net block utilisation and 13.00% IQF utilisation in FY26 (S1). The binding constraint is working capital (negative operating cash flow in all three years), and the issue sets nothing aside for it (S1, S2).

Earnings quality is unproven. Reported PAT has grown, but operating cash flow totalled about -₹2,632 lakh over FY24–FY26 (S2). Receivable days tripled from 26 to 77, and domestic receivables rose to ₹8,573.15 lakh, 88% of the total (S1). Management itself says the FY26 fall in material-cost ratio came from an inventory build-up that 'will reverse' (S1). Other income made up 22.97% of FY26 PBT (S1).

There is no moat. All raw material is bought order-to-order through commission agents, with no farm integration. India has about 646 MPEDA-registered shrimp processing units, and the company-commissioned industry report puts its share of the target market at 0.38% (S1). Revenue depends on China (31.29%) and on a customer list that shrank from 95 to 61, with the top ten now at 77.85% (S1, S2).

Governance and compliance history is poor for a company asking for public money. There were 31 late ROC filings, some over four years late, and processing was done outside the objects clause (S1). Promoter-linked entities sit on both the supply side (Green Asia Marine LLP) and the customer side (Green Asia Corp), and SG Exports was historically on both sides too. The RHP contradicts itself on whether promoters gave personal guarantees (S1).

The tax overhang and leverage leave little room for error. A ₹788.69 lakh s.68 demand is under appeal, and its pre-deposit has not been fully paid. Debt/equity is still 2.40x with ₹9,946.76 lakh of borrowings, mostly short-term packing credit (S1, S2). A shrimp downcycle, a China trade shock or a customer default would therefore hit a thinly capitalised balance sheet.

subsections.title: What Green Asia does and how it earns revenue

blocks.text: Green Asia Impex was incorporated on 5 August 2014 and is headquartered in Tadepalligudem, Andhra Pradesh. It buys, processes and sells frozen shrimp and dried red chillies to B2B customers: importers, distributors and food processors (S2). It converted to a public company in September 2025 and holds DGFT 'Two Star Export House' status (S1, S11). It began exporting shrimp to China in 2021. Until January 2023 it used third-party processing plants; that month its own shrimp plant came on stream (S1).

The revenue model is simple commodity processing. The company buys raw shrimp (mainly Vannamei, plus some Black Tiger and freshwater shrimp) and processes it into head-on, headless and peeled-deveined formats, frozen as blocks or IQF. It then sells on a per-order basis. Chilli is a smaller, seasonal trading-cum-processing line in Teja, Byadgi and Guntur Sannam varieties. Chillies are cleaned, de-stemmed, colour-sorted and packed (S1). Other operating revenue includes processing charges for third-party shrimp, cold-storage rent, duty drawback and sales of RoDTEP/MEIS scrips (S2).

blocks.caption: Revenue from operations by product and market (₹ lakh; source: RHP)

blocks.text: The company is presented as an exporter, but about 60% of revenue (59.79% in FY26) is domestic sales, mostly of shrimp (S1). The RHP does not say who the domestic buyers are. Its top-customer list shows that SG Exports, a firm the promoters were partners in until April 2024, was a major buyer (S1).

The only owned processing asset is the shrimp plant at Unguturu, Tadepalligudem (West Godavari). It sits on 1.43 acres with 1,838.76 sqm of built-up area. Installed capacity is 7,200 MTPA of block freezing plus 3,600 MTPA of IQF, 10,800 MTPA in total (S1, S2). The plant is semi-automated and has integrated cold storage at about -18°C (S1). Chilli processing takes place at a leased 1.30-acre unit in Vatticherukuru, Guntur, rented through Shanmukha Cotton Traders for ₹1.00 lakh a month. That work is largely manual, and finished chilli is stored in third-party warehouses (S1).

Block-freezing volumes have been flat for three years at about 3,800–4,000 MT gross. IQF, the value-added format, is ramping from a near-zero base (S1). The RHP gives chilli capacity as 1,500 MT but gives no production or utilisation figures, so the chilli line's operating scale cannot be checked (S1). The workforce is small: 136 permanent employees at 31 August 2026 and no contract labour (S1).

The supply chain runs end to end as follows. Raw shrimp and chilli are bought entirely through trader-cum-commission agents in Agricultural Market Committee markets, with no direct farmer sourcing in FY24–FY26 and no long-term contracts (S1). Shrimp arrives chilled below 4°C and is washed, graded, peeled, frozen, glazed, packed, metal-detected and cold-stored. It is then shipped on a 15–45 day processing cycle after order confirmation (S1). The company holds HACCP, ISO 22000, FSSAI, US FDA and China GACC registrations. The GACC registration is what makes the China business possible (S1, S2).

China is the anchor export market. It took ₹12,009.32 lakh, or 31.29% of FY26 revenue from operations: ₹10,780.91 lakh of shrimp and ₹1,228.41 lakh of chilli (S1, S2). Other FY26 export destinations were small: Kuwait (₹849.35 lakh), the USA (₹651.40 lakh), Malaysia, the UK, Vietnam and Thailand (S1). The US, the largest destination for Indian shrimp overall, contributed under 2% of shrimp revenue (S1).

blocks.text: Concentration is rising. The customer base shrank from 95 to 61 in FY26, and the top-ten share climbed to 77.85% (S1, S2). Supplier concentration is moderate: the top ten shrimp suppliers were 40.63% of shrimp purchases (S1). However, the largest FY26 shrimp supplier was promoter-linked Green Asia Marine LLP, and in FY24 the largest was SG Exports (S1). Chilli revenue swings sharply with Chinese buying. Chilli exports to China fell from ₹4,948.14 lakh in FY25 to ₹1,228.41 lakh in FY26, and chilli revenue fell 33.73% (S1).

Two related entities appear in the same cycle: a promoter-linked supplier (Green Asia Marine LLP) and a promoter-linked US buyer (Green Asia Corp, New Jersey). A former promoter firm (SG Exports) was historically both a customer and a supplier. As a result, part of the value chain is not arm's-length (S1).

India's seafood exports hit a record 19,72,018 MT worth ₹73,890.46 crore (US$8.46 billion) in FY26. Frozen shrimp alone was ₹49,037.93 crore across 7,92,647 MT, up 13.16% in rupees and 8.64% in dollars (S12, S21). The US is still the largest shrimp market at 2,56,128 MT, but its imports fell about 19.5% by volume in FY26. China was the second-largest shrimp buyer at 1,69,505 MT (S12). Growth came from non-US markets after the 2025 US tariff shock (S22).

The RHP's industry chapter comes from a Ken Research report that the company commissioned and paid for (S1, S2). It sizes India's shrimp market (domestic plus export) at ₹82,041 crore in FY25, projected to reach ₹1,28,400 crore by FY30 at a 9.4% CAGR. It sizes India's targeted shrimp export market at a slower ₹40,674 crore (CY25), growing to about ₹47,050 crore by 2030 at a 3.0% CAGR (S1). India dominates dried red chilli exports, with 79.5% of global export value in CY25 (US$1,314.1 million), and China took 35.4% of India's chilli exports (S1, S14). The same report projects the chilli export market to grow only 1.9% a year to FY30 (S1).

blocks.text: Trade-policy volatility is the main industry swing factor. Reports put the effective US duty on Indian shrimp near 58–59% after August 2025, and Crisil warned exports could fall 15–18% (S15). In February 2026 the US-India deal cut the reciprocal tariff to 18% (S13). Green Asia's exposure is mostly to China rather than the US, so China trade policy matters more for this company (S1).

The shrimp processing industry is crowded. The RHP itself cites 646 MPEDA-registered processing units, about 350 of them actively exporting (S1). Named shrimp peers include Devi Sea Foods, whose FY24 revenue of about ₹3,310 crore is nearly nine times Green Asia's. They also include Apex Frozen Foods (FY26 revenue about ₹931 crore), Jagadeesh Marine Exports, Kings Infra Ventures and Essex Marine (S1). Listed integrated players such as Avanti Feeds (about 22,000 MT of processing capacity) and Apex (a hatchery and 1,032 acres of farming plus about 9,240 MTPA of processing) control more of the chain (S16, S17). The named chilli peers, NK Agro Exports, Vijaya Krishna Spices and Siddhartha Corporation, are each larger than Green Asia's whole chilli line (S1).

No genuine moat is evident. The company does not own farms or hatcheries. It sources 100% through commission agents with no contracts. Its plant is small and under-utilised, and it holds only the standard certifications every exporting unit needs (S1). The industry report's own estimate of the company's obtainable market is ₹340 crore in 2025, 0.38% of the addressable market (S1). The RHP makes no import-substitution, sole-supplier or technology claim. Its listed 'strengths' (compliant facilities, relationships, agent network, experienced management) are generic (S1, S2).

Verdict on moat: none. This is a price-taking commodity processor in a fragmented industry. Industry processing margins run at 5–15% (S1), and Green Asia's EBITDA margin was 6.57% in FY26 (S2), at the low end of that range.

blocks.caption: Restated financials (₹ lakh; source: RHP/abridged prospectus)

blocks.text: Revenue grew at a 9.97% CAGR from FY24 to FY26 (S1). FY25 growth came from chilli exports to China, and FY26 growth from shrimp (shrimp revenue up 23.58%), which offset a 33.73% chilli decline (S1). New customers accounted for 94.26% of the FY26 revenue increase, a sign that growth depends on churn rather than on deepening existing accounts (S1).

Margin expansion has lower quality than the headline suggests. Management states that the FY26 fall in cost of materials, from 86.72% to 83.94% of revenue, reflects an inventory build-up credit and 'not a reduction in the cost of procurement'. It adds that this benefit 'will reverse' when the stock is sold (S1). Other income more than doubled to ₹483.10 lakh, or 22.97% of PBT (S1). Finance costs rose 95.56%, driven by bank charges on foreign-currency packing credit, which went from ₹62.82 lakh to ₹575.55 lakh (S1).
The high ROE (46–51%) reflects a very thin equity base and heavy debt more than exceptional economics. Net worth was only ₹1,546.28 lakh in FY24 against borrowings of ₹6,373.43 lakh (S2).

blocks.caption: Balance sheet and cash flow (₹ lakh; source: RHP/abridged prospectus)

blocks.text: This is the core problem. Over FY24–FY26 the company reported about ₹3,262 lakh of cumulative PAT but consumed about ₹2,632 lakh of operating cash, and financed the gap with debt (S2). Receivable days rose from 26 to 49 to 77, and inventory days from 85 to 114 (S1). The company extended export credit from about 90 to 120 days in FY25. In FY26 the entire receivables increase came from domestic customers: domestic receivables jumped from ₹3,426.13 lakh to ₹8,573.15 lakh, 88% of the total (S1). It also wrote off ₹145.66 lakh of debit balances in FY26 (S1).

Liquidity is thin. Year-end cash was just ₹52.65 lakh against ₹9,181.07 lakh of short-term borrowings (S1). By 31 August 2026 total outstanding debt had risen to ₹11,197.37 lakh, including new term loans of ₹1,296.95 lakh taken after March 2026 (S1). The working-capital lines are secured on stock and debtors plus promoter personal guarantees, and the term loans on property, including the MD's personal property (S1).

Red flag: the gap between cash flow and profit. Operating cash flow was negative in all three years while profit rose each year, and receivables grew almost 4x in two years. Until the company shows it can turn profit into cash, the reported earnings should be discounted (S1, S2).

subsections.title: Does the trend support the growth story?

blocks.text: Only partly. Revenue and PAT are rising and leverage is falling (S2). However, the growth has been bought with working capital (net working capital days 52 to 90), a shrinking customer base (95 to 61), and a margin boost that management itself calls temporary (S1). Physical block-freezing output has been flat at about 3,800–4,000 MT gross for three years. Revenue growth therefore came from IQF ramp-up, prices and mix, not from filling the plant (S1).

items: Positive: PAT up about 2.3x in two years, and equity more than doubled (S2).
Negative: the reported numbers include a large tax dispute over 'unexplained credits' for AY 2022-23 (S1).
Negative: auditors raised no qualification, but the accounts are under Indian GAAP rather than Ind AS (S1, S2).
Neutral: no dividend history (S10).

sections.title: Issue details and objects of the issue

blocks.text: The issue is a book-built SME offer of up to ₹6,010 lakh, listing on NSE Emerge. It comprises a fresh issue of up to ₹5,310 lakh and an offer for sale of up to ₹700 lakh by the two promoters: Pasupuleti Venkata Ramarao ₹370 lakh and Pasupuleti Meenakshi ₹330 lakh (S2). The fresh issue was cut from its DRHP size after a pre-IPO placement of 6,71,045 shares at ₹77, which raised ₹516.70 lakh and has already been spent in the ordinary course of business (S1, S2).

blocks.text: Secondary sites disagree on the exact share counts (for example 58.94 lakh vs 59.00 lakh vs 55.58 lakh fresh shares) (S5, S7, S18). The rupee amounts in the RHP (₹5,310 lakh fresh, ₹700 lakh OFS) are the reliable figures (S2). The task brief described the price band as not yet known. The ₹85–90 band comes from secondary sources and the company's own press release (S5, S6).

blocks.caption: Use of net proceeds and project cost (₹ lakh; source: RHP)
rows: [●] – capped at lower of 15% of gross fresh issue or ₹1,000 lakh

blocks.text: Of the ₹5,310 lakh fresh issue, ₹4,002.77 lakh (about 75%) is earmarked for one project: a second shrimp processing plant of about 4,955.69 sqm at Chinnayagudem, East Godavari. It would add 11,100 MTPA and take total capacity to about 21,900 MTPA (S1, S2). Nothing is set aside for debt repayment or working capital, even though the business is working-capital-hungry and has had negative operating cash flow (S1). The ₹700 lakh OFS goes to the promoters, not the company (S2).

items: No machinery orders have been placed. Everything rests on quotations dated August–September 2026, some valid for only 30 days. About ₹1,065 lakh of it is priced in US dollars from a Vietnamese supplier, so the cost carries currency risk (S1).
There is no contingency provision in the project cost. Taxes, duties and any overrun must come from internal accruals, for a company whose operating cash flow is negative (S1).
Timeline: excavation October 2026, machinery orders March–April 2027, trial run January–February 2028, commercial production April 2028 (S1).

Approvals: consent to establish and factory licence are received. Panchayat NOC, fire NOC, water and DTCP layout approvals are in process. The power connection and consent to operate have not yet been applied for (S1).
No bank or financial institution has appraised the project. Brickwork Ratings is the monitoring agency (S1).

blocks.text: The capacity logic is questionable. The existing plant ran at 38.38% net block utilisation and 13.00% IQF utilisation in FY26 (S1). The only support for demand is the paid industry report's claim that 'the present demand pipeline is already 2–3x the existing capacity', and the RHP discloses no order book (S1).

The promoters are a married couple. Pasupuleti Venkata Ramarao (52, BSc Andhra University) is Managing Director, with over 13 years in seafood and dry-chilli exports. Pasupuleti Meenakshi (42, higher-secondary education) is Executive Director, with over 6 years in the business (S1, S2). Together they hold 92.02%, with another 2.63% held by family members in the promoter group (S2). The MD also sits on the boards of Green Asia Cold Storages, Green Asia Corp (USA) and the Chillies Exporters Association India (S1).

blocks.text: The board is new and assembled for the IPO. The CFO, company secretary and all independent directors joined in 2025 or later, and no director has served on a listed-company board (S1). Two independent directors resigned within two months of appointment, citing 'temporary unavailability', and were reappointed later (S1). Another independent director, Vishnu Chavda, joined and left within four months in 2025 (S1). The MD is also linked to a struck-off company, Clarion Park Solutions (S1).
This is not a routine RPT section. Promoter-linked entities sit on both sides of the trade (S1).

blocks.caption: Material related-party items (₹ lakh; source: RHP Note 28 / RF44)
rows: Sold for 135.75 (set off vs promoter loans)

items: In FY24 SG Exports, a partnership of the promoters, was the largest shrimp customer (25.24% of revenue) and the largest supplier (S1). The promoters retired from it 'for personal reasons' on 13 April 2024, the start of the first year shown on a non-related basis. The firm remained a top customer afterwards (S1).

The company sold its wholly-owned cold-storage subsidiary to the promoters for ₹135.75 lakh. The price was not paid in cash; it was set off against the company's loans owed to them. The company then advanced that entity ₹274.53 lakh as a 'supplier' in FY26 (S1).
The RHP says there are 'no common pursuits' with group companies, but Green Asia Marine LLP supplies shrimp and Green Asia Corp buys it (S1).
The RHP contradicts itself on guarantees. One page says the promoters have given no personal guarantees; the indebtedness section says they guarantee the Union Bank and ICICI facilities (S1).

blocks.text: The compliance record is poor. The RHP discloses 31 late ROC filings, including a DPT-3 filed 1,887 days late, Meenakshi's DIR-12 regularisation 1,558 days late, and AOC-4 annual accounts filed 1,267, 670 and 230 days late. The company attributes this to having no full-time company secretary (S1). It processed goods from FY23 while its objects clause did not permit manufacturing or processing. It amended the clause only on 20 September 2025, and its first condonation filing was rejected before a second was approved (S1). Statutory dues (TDS, PF, etc.) were paid late by up to 142 days (S1). The original TAN allotment letter cannot be traced (S1).

Litigation is limited to tax matters, but the amounts are material. Four tax proceedings against the company total ₹954.06 lakh, led by a ₹901.19 lakh income-tax demand for AY 2022 (S1, S2). The contingent-liability note shows a ₹788.69 lakh demand arising from s.68 (unexplained cash credits) and s.41(1) additions, now before CIT(Appeals) (S1). Of the ₹78.87 lakh pre-deposit, ₹24.62 lakh remains unpaid, and the company has sought time until 31 December 2026 citing cash-flow constraints (S1). There are no criminal, SEBI or regulatory proceedings against the promoters (S2).

blocks.text: SME lock-ins are shorter than mainboard ones. Half of the promoters' excess holding and all pre-IPO placement shares, bought at ₹77, can be sold one year after listing (S1).

items: Cash conversion: operating cash flow was negative in FY24, FY25 and FY26, receivable days rose from 26 to 77, and domestic receivables reached ₹8,573.15 lakh (S1, S2). If collections slip further, lenders, not shareholders, control the outcome.

China concentration: 31.29% of revenue came from China in FY26, and chilli exports to China collapsed from ₹4,948.14 lakh to ₹1,228.41 lakh in a single year. That shows how quickly this demand can disappear (S1).
Customer concentration and churn: the top ten customers per segment were 77.85% of revenue, and the customer count fell from 95 to 61 (S1, S2).

Execution on the IPO-funded plant: no machinery orders, several approvals pending, no contingency provision, a USD-priced equipment quote and an April 2028 start. Meanwhile the existing plant is about 38% utilised (net block) (S1).
Tax dispute: a ₹788.69–901.19 lakh income-tax demand relating to unexplained credits is under appeal. That is roughly 19–22% of FY26 net worth (S1).

Leverage and covenants: ₹11,197.37 lakh of debt outstanding at 31 August 2026, mostly packing credit backed by promoter guarantees. Lender consent is needed for dividends and changes in management or shareholding (S1).
Governance: a history of long-delayed filings, operating outside its objects clause, promoter-linked counterparties on both sides of trade, and internal contradictions in the RHP (S1).
Biosecurity and commodity risk: shrimp disease (e.g. White Spot), weather, seasonality and raw-material price swings, with no supplier contracts and no formal FX hedging policy (S1, S2).

blocks.text: Many of these risks compound one another. A China demand shock would hit a thinly capitalised, debt-funded business at the same time as a large tax appeal and a capex programme that has no contingency buffer.

items: Only 49.60% of property, plant and equipment is insured (₹765.06 lakh of ₹1,542.51 lakh) (S1).
The chilli facility is leased, and the lease end date is misprinted in the RHP (S1).
All operations are in Andhra Pradesh, which is exposed to cyclones and floods (S1).
The industry report was paid for by the company (S1, S2).
The RHP's internal inconsistencies include promoter-group holding (98.95% vs 94.65%), pre-IPO allotment dates, MD remuneration, and the tax demand figure (S1).

blocks.text: The DRHP's generic risks (Indian macro conditions, listing delays, rating downgrades) apply to every issuer and are not decision-relevant here (S1).

Management's concrete plans are in the RHP. Its growth strategies are capacity expansion at Chinnayagudem, value addition in shrimp (IQF, semi-cooked, portion-controlled and ready-to-cook products), cost efficiency, and new geographies (S1, S2). For shrimp it names South Korea, Russia and the EU as target markets; for chilli, Vietnam, Malaysia, the US and Europe (S1). The new plant is targeted for commercial production in April 2028 (S1).

In the IPO press release, MD Pasupuleti Venkata Rama Rao said the company's focus 'will remain on strengthening our processing capabilities, expanding our product portfolio and enhancing our presence across domestic as well as international markets' (S6). This is a generic statement. Management has given no revenue, margin, or utilisation guidance, and the RHP discloses no order book (S1, S6).

The most quantitative forward view is in the commissioned Ken Research report. It projects the company's 'serviceable obtainable market' rising from ₹340 crore in 2025 to ₹1,470 crore by 2030 (S1). That is a consultant's addressable-market estimate paid for by the issuer, not management guidance, and should be treated accordingly.

Near-term takeaway: the IPO proceeds add no capacity before FY29. FY27 and FY28 results will depend on the existing plant, chilli seasonality, China demand, and whether the company can collect its receivables (S1).

subsections.title: Sector backdrop for the next two years

blocks.text: The backdrop is mixed. Indian shrimp exports grew to a record in FY26 despite a fall in US volume, helped by stronger China, EU and Southeast Asian demand (S12, S22). The US tariff cut to 18% in February 2026 removes some of the worst-case pressure (S13). The paid industry report still forecasts only about 3% a year growth in India's targeted shrimp export market and 1.9% in chilli exports to 2030 (S1). Any growth well above that would have to come from market-share gains, which is hard for a sub-scale, non-integrated processor.

subsections.title: Demand so far (partial – issue closes 28 September 2026)

blocks.caption: Subscription at day 2 close, 5:34 PM, 25 September 2026 (S7)

blocks.text: By the day-2 close, bids covered 1,61,600 shares against 63,48,800 offered, from 49 applications (S7). A tracker checked on 27 September showed the same 49 applications as of 26 September, and the issue remained undersubscribed (S8). 26–27 September was a weekend, so the final day, 28 September, will decide the outcome. These figures are partial and should not be read as final demand.

No anchor investor allocation was found in any source reviewed (S5, S11). Grey-market premium trackers showed either no trading or a GMP of ₹0 (S9, S10, S11). These figures are unofficial and are not treated as an investment signal. The weak demand, particularly from QIBs, is consistent with the concerns in this report, but the verdict does not rest on it.

method: Primary sources: the Red Herring Prospectus dated 18 September 2026 and the Abridged Prospectus, both downloaded from the company's IPO-documents page (S4) and read directly. The abridged prospectus was read in full. The RHP was read section by section: risk factors, the offer, capital structure, objects, industry overview, business, history, management, promoters, restated financial statements (including the related-party note), MD&A, indebtedness, litigation and approvals. Figures come from the restated consolidated financials (Indian GAAP; consolidated only because a subsidiary was held until April 2024). The February 2026 DRHP on NSE's archive (S3) timed out when fetched and was not read; the later RHP supersedes it. Subscription (day 2 only; the issue closes 28 September), GMP and issue-structure details come from secondary sites (S5, S7–S11, S18), whose share counts differ slightly. The RHP rupee amounts were used as authoritative. The task brief said the price band was not yet known; secondary sources and the company press release report ₹85–90. Industry data combines the company-paid Ken Research report in the RHP with MPEDA-based news reports (S12, S20, S21). Some news items (S15, S20, S21, S22) were seen only in search-result snippets because the pages blocked fetching. No anchor-investor disclosure was found. Valuation (P/E, peer multiples) was deliberately excluded. The RHP contains several internal inconsistencies (promoter-group holding, personal guarantees, pre-IPO allotment date, MD remuneration, tax demand amount); these are flagged in the text rather than resolved.
